main_damage_causes: Dudley's calculated psychological manipulation and deliberate cruelty are consistently softened into generic comic-relief spoiled-child behaviour, losing the specificity that makes him a compelling antagonist.

The film removes or compresses the key scenes showing Harry gaining power over Dudley (the garden magic-threat scene, the Dementor alley moral complexity), flattening the evolution of their dynamic and reducing Harry's domestic agency.

Dudley's interior life — glimpsed through the Dementor's effect on him and culminating in his farewell — is largely absent from the film corpus, which means his redemption arc is either entirely lost or lands without the necessary groundwork.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film 1 (Sorcerer's Stone) - Zoo birthday scene: Dudley wakes Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Dudley as a calculating bully who uses fake crying to manipulate his parents, throws tantrums about present counts, and actively excludes Harry. He punches Harry in the ribs at the snake tank ('Out of the way, you,' he said, punching Harry in the ribs). His cruelty is deliberate and premeditated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dudley cheerfully wakes Harry by jumping on the stairs above his cupboard and calling out 'Wake up, cousin! We're going to the zoo!' — a moment of almost playful energy rather than contemptuous exclusion. The film omits Dudley punching Harry at the snake tank; instead Dudley simply shoves him aside without the explicit violence of the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dudley is a deliberate, physically abusive bully from the very first scenes. Opening with a cheerful wake-up call softens his introduction and removes the physical cruelty at the zoo that establishes his character. The punch in the ribs is the direct cause of Harry falling and the glass vanishing — its absence mildly weakens the causal chain and the sense of Dudley's casual violence.

damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Dudley counts 36 presents, goes 'red in the face,' and his parents immediately capitulate with promises of two more presents, then 39 total. He does hard mental arithmetic slowly ('Thirty... thirty...'), revealing dim-wittedness alongside entitled manipulation. His fake crying is explicitly noted: 'it had been years since he'd really cried — but he knew that if he screwed up his face and wailed, his mother would give him anything he wanted.' The tantrum is a masterclass in weaponised helplessness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the present-counting complaint and Petunia's capitulation but compresses and softens it. The slow, laborious arithmetic ('thirty... thirty...') and the explicit authorial note about fake crying are absent. The scene plays as a simple spoiled-child moment rather than exposing Dudley's calculated manipulation of his parents.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's tantrum scene reveals Dudley as not just spoiled but strategically manipulative — he performs emotion to extract reward. Losing the fake-crying detail and the dim arithmetic removes a layer of characterisation that distinguishes him from a generic spoiled child.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film 1 (Sorcerer's Stone) - Hagrid's hut: Dudley eats Harry's birthday cake
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has no equivalent moment of Dudley eating Harry's cake during Hagrid's visit. Dudley is terrified and hides behind his parents. His characterisation in this scene is cowardice and greed (he fidgets at the sausages), and the pig-tail is Hagrid's punishment for Vernon's insult — accidentally aimed at Dudley.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film adds a visual gag in which Dudley, unnoticed by everyone, steals and eats Harry's birthday cake while the adults argue. This is a film-original invention presenting Dudley as a comic glutton rather than a frightened, cowardly bully.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While minor, the film replaces Dudley's book-accurate terror and cowardice with a comedic gluttony beat not present in the corpus. It shifts his register from threatening-bully-turned-coward to simple comic relief, slightly undercutting the fear Hagrid inspires in him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film 2 (Chamber of Secrets) - Dudley's 'birthday' taunt through the metal flap
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 209: Dudley taunts Harry in the garden on his birthday — 'Today's your birthday. How come you haven't got any cards? Haven't you even got friends at that freak place?' He does this face-to-face, in the open, and Harry responds with confidence, fake-threatening him with magic ('Jiggery pokery! Hocus pocus squiggly wiggly!'). Dudley panics and flees, howling for his mother. The scene demonstrates Harry's growing ability to turn the tables and Dudley's deep fear of magic.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9/13: Dudley delivers the birthday taunt ('I know what day it is... Today's your birthday. And nobody cares.') by sliding a bowl of soup through the metal flap in Harry's locked bedroom door and snapping it shut — a much more safely distanced, sneering cruelty with no risk of retaliation. Harry cannot respond or turn the tables; he simply sighs. The power dynamic heavily favours Dudley.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is important because it shows Harry now has leverage over Dudley — the threat of magic makes Dudley flee screaming. This is a key beat in their evolving dynamic, showing Harry is no longer entirely powerless at Privet Drive. The film instead shows Harry completely imprisoned and humiliated with no ability to respond, which reverses the dynamic and removes Harry's small domestic agency. It also loses the comedy of Dudley's irrational terror.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film 3 (Prisoner of Azkaban) - Dementor alleyway scene: Dudley's characterisation before the attack
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 378-418: Before the Dementors arrive, Dudley and Harry have an extended, psychologically rich confrontation. Dudley is now a Junior Heavyweight Boxing Champion, physically formidable, leading a gang that has been beating up younger children ('He was sixteen... and he was out cold for twenty minutes'). He taunts Harry with knowledge of Harry's nightmares about Cedric — 'Don't kill Cedric! Dad, help me, Dad!'— demonstrating genuine cruelty and perceptiveness. Harry feels 'fourteen years' hatred' and is genuinely tempted to use his wand. Dudley also lands a punch that lifts Harry off his feet. The confrontation is morally complex: Harry is the one who pulls his wand first.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 14: The film compresses this into a brief exchange. Dudley taunts Harry about beating up a 10-year-old and mockingly imitates Harry's nightmare ('Don't kill Cedric! Who's Cedric, your boyfriend?'). The exchange is shorter, the boxing champion context is reduced to a throwaway mention ('Hey, Big D'), and the physical punch that knocks Harry down is absent. The moral complexity of Harry nearly jinxing Dudley is reduced.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's pre-Dementor scene gives Dudley genuine menace — he is physically dangerous and psychologically perceptive enough to weaponise Harry's trauma. The film retains the Cedric taunt but loses the physical threat, the extended power dynamic, and Harry's morally ambiguous near-jinxing. Dudley reads as a generic bully rather than a formidable, evolving antagonist.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film 3 (Prisoner of Azkaban) - Dementor attack aftermath: Dudley's interior experience
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 476-484: After the Dementor attack, Dudley gives a remarkable account of his experience — 'All went dark... And then I h-heard... things. Inside m-my head.' He cannot articulate what he heard (his worst memories), and Harry wonders with genuine curiosity what spoiled, pampered Dudley's worst memories could be. This is one of the few moments that hints Dudley may have inner depths — that even his life of privilege contains something he finds unbearable. His slow, traumatised testimony is psychologically significant.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 14: After the attack, Dudley is shown collapsed on the floor, then Vernon and Petunia fuss over him. The film has no equivalent of Dudley's stumbling verbal account of what the Dementor made him experience. The audience never hears him describe hearing things inside his head or the implication that he too has painful memories.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the first crack in Dudley's one-dimensional characterisation — the suggestion that beneath the bullying and greed there is genuine interior suffering. Its absence means the film Dudley never becomes even slightly sympathetic or three-dimensional, which makes his arc in Deathly Hallows (if filmed) land without preparation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film 7 Part 1 (Deathly Hallows) - Dudley's farewell and handshake
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 561-609: Dudley's farewell is a carefully constructed emotional arc. He initiates by asking why Harry isn't coming with them, grapples visibly with thoughts 'too unwieldy for expression,' says unprompted 'I don't think you're a waste of space,' acknowledges 'You saved my life,' and finally extends his hand for a handshake. Harry is 'embarrassed and astonished.' The scene is the payoff of Dudley's entire arc — the boy who bullied Harry for sixteen years shows the first genuine human decency. Harry notes the cup of cold tea on the landing may not have been a booby trap after all.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus for Deathly Hallows Part 1 (Scene 15) contains only the Snatchers scene and forest sequences — the Privet Drive farewell scene does not appear in the provided film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dudley's farewell handshake and 'I don't think you're a waste of space' is the single most important scene in his entire arc — it is his redemption moment, the payoff for sixteen years of cruelty, and evidence that the Dementor attack genuinely changed him. Since this scene does not appear in the provided film corpus, its absence (whether cut or simply not in the corpus) represents the most structurally damaging loss for his character. Without it, Dudley ends the saga as an unredeemed bully. The book explicitly frames this as meaningful: Harry himself is moved, and his last thought about Dudley is warmth.
